summary: This Standards Track document presents two YANG 1.1 modules with reusable groupings for configuring UDP clients and UDP servers.

eli5.summary: Ready-made building blocks for describing how a computer sends and receives UDP messages, so people need not rewrite them.

questions: what is the ietf-udp-client yang module
what does the udp-server grouping contain
how to configure a udp server in yang
subtitle: Reusable YANG building blocks for describing how a UDP client or UDP server is configured.

tldr.problem: Many protocols that run over UDP each need configuration for where to send datagrams or which addresses and ports to listen on, and each YANG model would otherwise redefine the same nodes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9984 defines two YANG 1.1 modules, ietf-udp-client and ietf-udp-server, each with one reusable grouping: udp-client (remote address and port, optional local binding) and udp-server (a list of local address and port bind points).
tldr.outcome: Other YANG modules can pull in these groupings instead of writing their own UDP settings. The modules define no data nodes by themselves, so they add no extra security exposure.

today: RFC 9984 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the definition of the ietf-udp-client and ietf-udp-server modules.

sections.title: What the Document Provides
sections.content:
RFC 9984 presents two YANG 1.1 modules with reusable groupings for managing UDP clients and UDP servers, where UDP is the protocol of RFC 768. A grouping is a named bundle of configuration nodes that other modules can include.

The modules may be used directly, to define a specific UDP client or server, or together with the configuration of higher-level protocols that depend on UDP. The document also states that it complies with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) and defines no protocol-accessible nodes that are config false.
sections.eli5: It is a box of ready-made pieces for describing how a computer talks over UDP, so nobody has to rebuild them.

sections.title: The udp-client Grouping
sections.content:
The ietf-udp-client module defines the udp-client grouping, which gives a UDP client information about the remote server. It has four nodes: remote-address, remote-port, local-address and local-port.

The remote-address is mandatory and may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a hostname. The remote-port has neither a default nor a mandatory statement. Modules that use the grouping SHOULD refine it with a default when the port is well known, or with mandatory when a port must always be configured.

The two local nodes sit behind a feature called local-binding, which says the client supports configuring the local address and local port. The local-port defaults to 0, meaning the operating system may pick any port. The local and remote addresses SHOULD be from the same address family in normal operation; differences may occur in abnormal or error conditions, so they are allowed to be reported.
sections.eli5: The client form asks where to send messages and, if you want, which of your own doors and numbers to send from. If you leave your own number as zero, the computer picks one.

sections.title: Client and Server Examples
sections.content:
The client example in the RFC sets remote-address to www.example.com, remote-port to 10000, local-address to 192.0.2.2 and local-port to 12345. The outer udp-client element is only a stand-in: it does not exist in the data model and simulates the grouping being a container.

The server examples show a server listening on one IPv4 address, 192.0.2.2 port 49152, and a server listening on that IPv4 address together with an IPv6 address, 2001:db8::0 port 49153. Examples are written in XML, though the RFC notes other encodings such as JSON could be used.
sections.eli5: The examples are filled-in forms: one client that names who to talk to, and servers that say which addresses and numbers they wait at.

sections.title: The udp-server Grouping
sections.content:
The ietf-udp-server module defines the udp-server grouping for managing UDP servers. Its core is a list called local-bind, keyed by local-address, with at least one element. Each entry is a bind (listen) point holding a mandatory local-address and an optional local-port.

A server instance may have several bind points, for example the same port number in different address families or different port numbers in the same address family. The local-address may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a wildcard (0.0.0.0 or ::), so the server can listen on any address. As in the client grouping, local-port has no default or mandatory statement, and users of the grouping SHOULD refine it in the same way.

Both groupings use fairly typical node names, so stacking several uses statements can cause name conflicts. The consuming model is expected to resolve this, for example by wrapping the uses statement in a container; the modules deliberately do not do it themselves, for maximum flexibility.
sections.eli5: A server can wait at several doors at once. The server form is a list of those doors, each with an address and a number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are designed to be accessed through YANG-based management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF. Those protocols have to use a secure transport layer (for example SSH, TLS or QUIC) and have to use mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict which users may reach which operations and content.

The modules define identities, types and groupings meant for reuse, and by themselves expose no writable data nodes, no read-only state and no RPCs. So they raise no additional security issues. Modules that reuse the groupings should state their own security considerations, since nodes such as remote-address, remote-port, local-address and local-port can expose privacy-related information.
sections.eli5: The forms are blank, so they hold no secrets. Whoever fills them in must protect them, because addresses and numbers can say a lot about a computer.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has assigned two URIs in the IETF XML Registry, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-udp-client and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-udp-server, each with the IESG as registrant contact.

IANA has also registered the two module names in the YANG Module Names registry. ietf-udp-client uses the prefix udpc and ietf-udp-server uses the prefix udps. Neither is maintained by IANA, and both cite RFC 9984. Both modules carry the revision date 2026-06-15 and import types from RFC 9911.
sections.eli5: The names of the two forms were written in an official list so nobody else uses the same names.
